topic: Back pain after deadlifts: what to change

slides.headline: Deadlifts left your back sore?
slides.sub: Most gym back tweaks settle. Here's what to change in your training.

slides.title: Most gym back tweaks settle
slides.body: A sore back after lifting is common and usually a strain, not damage. Most people improve noticeably within days to a couple of weeks with gentle movement and a few smart training changes.

slides.title: Drop the load, keep the pattern
slides.body: Rather than stopping altogether, keep practising the hinge with a load that feels comfortably light. Staying in the movement pattern tends to help both your confidence and your recovery.

slides.title: Look at your total volume
slides.body: Flare-ups often follow a jump in load, sets or frequency, or a big session on poor sleep. Build back gradually, adding weight over weeks rather than chasing your old numbers straight away.

slides.title: Try a friendlier variation
slides.body: Trap bar deadlifts, block pulls or lighter Romanian deadlifts can feel easier while things settle. Pick the variation you can do with little or no pain, then build from there.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked promptly if pain spreads down the leg with numbness or weakness, you notice changes in bladder or bowel control, or pain is severe, constant and not easing after a week or two.

slides.headline: Want to get back under the bar?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your lift, your load and your back, then map out a gradual return plan that fits your program.

caption:
Tweaked your back on deadlifts? You probably don't need to stop lifting.

Most gym back pain is a strain, not damage, and it usually settles within days to a couple of weeks. The trick is to keep moving: practise the hinge with a comfortably light load, cut back total volume, and try a friendlier variation like trap bar deadlifts or block pulls while things calm down. Then build the weight back over weeks, not days.

Get checked promptly if pain spreads down the leg with numbness or weakness, if you notice bladder or bowel changes, or if pain is severe and not easing.
